idiom_name: command objects + command repository (queue) + concrete command processor (scheduler) + supplier/receiver
implementation_notes: Give every request a uniform Command interface with an execute operation (and an inverse where undo is promised). The processor, not the client, owns the repository: clients hand commands over and stop there. The concrete processor decides scheduling - a single-threaded loop for deterministic ordering, a worker pool for throughput, a dispatcher for deferred or prioritised work - and appends executed commands to a history that backs undo, redo and macros. Keep receivers (suppliers) out of the client's hands, keep commands immutable values, bound the repository with an explicit overflow policy, and give commands identity (idempotency/dedupe keys) so retries and replay are safe. Add the services - log, undo, macro, priority - inside the processor, not in the client or receiver.
code_sketch:
client:   cmd = PlaceOrder(order_id, qty)      # request reified; receiver not named
          processor.push(cmd)                        # queued, returns immediately
processor (concrete):
  loop:
      cmd = repository.take()                       # scheduling/priority policy
      cmd.execute(supplier)                         # receiver does the work
      history.append(cmd)                           # logging / undo / macro support
pitfalls: Letting the client keep a reference to the receiver and run the work itself: that recreates the coupling the pattern removes.
An unbounded repository presented as resilience - it converts overload into memory growth; bound it and define what happens when it is full.
Confusing the command history with the domain event log; replaying a recorded command re-executes its effects unless commands are idempotent.
Executing a command while holding the repository lock, which serialises all workers and deadlocks as soon as a command enqueues another command.

Wrong move: route every trivial CRUD operation through a command + dedicated handler (the default MediatR/CQRS reflex) -> the codebase inflates into one command class, one handler and DTOs per operation, call sites lose sight of the logic and simple apps gain pure ceremony; instead keep direct service calls for trivial operations and reserve the processor for requests that genuinely need queueing, undo, logging or scheduling.

Wrong move: dispatch commands fire-and-forget and treat 'accepted' as success -> a handler exception vanishes into the processor and callers build private retry/timeout layers on top; instead return a future/result per command (as Axon's CommandBus.dispatch does) and record failures against the command id.

Wrong move: leave the undo history unbounded, one entry per keystroke -> long sessions exhaust memory and undo becomes useless noise; instead coalesce successive same-type commands and cap the history (as NSUndoManager's setLevelsOfUndo: does), dropping the oldest groups.
